title: Hymn and Portrait
premise: Folklorist Lena Dravenmoor arrives at Hollowmere to record a lullaby that villagers will only sing once, discovering that each performance feeds something that counts the singers. When the mirrors in her family's rented house begin lagging a second behind reality, Lena realizes the thing has chosen her household, and that the lag is a countdown. Refusing to believe even as belief becomes survival, she uncovers that the village's founding families sold their reflections generations ago and have been hiding ever since. In the end, Lena sings the lullaby a second time herself, trading her own memory of her family to buy them escape, and walks out of Hollowmere a stranger to the people she saved.
about_author: Casper Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing funeral hymns in remote coastal villages before turning to fiction. They write in the margins of old songbooks and claim their best ideas arrive a second after they do.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Lena Dravenmoor arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing an old woman who sings a lullaby exactly once, then goes pale and refuses to repeat it. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: intrigued condescension curdling into unease.

chapters.title: House on Lagging Lane
chapters.summary: Lena moves her family—brother Theo and niece Ivy—into a rented cottage on the village edge. Ivy mentions the mirrors 'feel slow,' which Lena dismisses as a child's imagination. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: warm domestic normalcy undercut by a first hairline crack.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Lena tests the hallway mirror with a stopwatch and confirms the reflection lags exactly one second. Theo accuses her of staging a prank; the recording of the old woman's lullaby plays back with an extra voice humming underneath. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: rationalist denial beginning to strain.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Digging in parish archives, Lena finds a ledger of 'counts'—lists of names tallied after every recorded singing, some struck through. The last count is dated the week the previous tenants vanished. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: scholarly thrill shading into dread.

chapters.title: What Ivy Saw
chapters.summary: Ivy's POV: the child describes the mirror-girl who copies her but smiles a half-second wrong, and who has started waving first. Lena comforts Ivy while privately checking her own reflection for that smile. Emotional beat: protective tenderness laced with quiet horror.

chapters.title: The Villagers' Silence
chapters.summary: Lena confronts the village council, who deny the lullaby exists while their own portraits' eyes seem freshly painted. An elder, Maren, privately warns: 'It counts what answers it. Stop answering.' POV: Lena. Emotional beat: frustration at institutional denial turning to fear.

chapters.title: Reflections of the Missing
chapters.summary: Theo, home alone, sees his own reflection continue moving after he stops—picking up Lena's hairbrush, smiling at nothing. He tells no one, but begins sleeping with the mirrors covered. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: bravado collapsing into isolation and dread.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: The delay grows to three seconds. In the mirror, Lena watches her reflection set down a cup she hasn't finished holding, and realizes the reflection is rehearsing. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: the moment denial becomes impossible.

chapters.title: Maren's Confession
chapters.summary: Maren reveals the founding families sold their reflections to the Counting Thing for prosperity, and the lullaby is the payment schedule—each singing names the next household. Her own family's portraits have been empty for a century. POV: Lena with Maren. Emotional beat: grief and complicity.

chapters.title: Portraits in the Attic
chapters.summary: Lena finds the cottage attic lined with portraits of every previous tenant, faces scratched out except the eyes, which are mirrors. One portrait's eyes show Ivy's room, live. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: violation—the house itself is a trap.

chapters.title: Running Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: The family attempts to leave; every road loops back to Hollowmere, and the car radio plays the lullaby in Ivy's recorded hum. They return to the cottage as dusk falls. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: panic, helplessness, the geography of the trap.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Analyzing the recording, Lena isolates the under-hum: it's her own voice, singing words she's never learned, in a dialect dead for two hundred years. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: identity beginning to dissolve at the edges.

chapters.title: Bargaining with Glass
chapters.summary: Lena speaks to her reflection directly, demanding terms. The reflection answers a beat early now, and offers a deal: one singer, freely given, and the count closes. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: desperate negotiation, the horror of negotiating with yourself.

chapters.title: Ivy's Lullaby
chapters.summary: Ivy's POV: the mirror-girl teaches Ivy the lullaby's second verse, sweetly, patiently. Ivy sings it to her dolls, and every doll's painted eyes go glassy and dark. Emotional beat: innocence weaponized, heartbreak.

chapters.title: The Village Remembers
chapters.summary: Maren gathers the villagers to sing the lullaby together and overload the count—a ritual that failed once before, in 1843, at the cost of forty names. Lena finds the 1843 tally: Maren's signature at the top. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with understanding.

chapters.title: Broken Mirrors, Broken Rules
chapters.summary: Theo smashes every mirror in the cottage; the shards each reflect a different room, and in one, a version of Lena who never came to Hollowmere waves goodbye. The lag stops—for one night. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: defiant hope, false dawn.

chapters.title: The Thing That Counts
chapters.summary: The lag returns as ten seconds. In the mirror, Lena watches the reflection of the room fill with tall, patient figures holding ledgers, waiting. They have no faces because they gave them away. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: awe and terror—the scale of the debt revealed.

chapters.title: Verse Three
chapters.summary: Lena deciphers the lullaby's third verse from the 1843 ledger: it isn't a payment, it's a lock—a binding song that requires a singer who remembers nothing of what they love. She understands the price before she understands the plan. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: cold clarity, sacrificial resolve.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Count
chapters.summary: The family's last ordinary night. Theo and Ivy sleep; Lena memorizes their faces, deliberately, like a scholar memorizing a text she intends to lose. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness, farewell without goodbye.

chapters.title: Hymn
chapters.summary: At dawn, Lena sings the lullaby complete, all three verses, into the great mirror. The Counting Thing accepts her memory as payment; the portraits' eyes go dark one by one, and the roads open. POV: Lena, memory unraveling mid-song. Emotional beat: climax—sacrifice enacted in real time.

chapters.title: Portrait
chapters.summary: A woman walks out of Hollowmere carrying a songbook she cannot read and a car key she cannot explain. Theo and Ivy, waiting at the village edge, approach the stranger who looks exactly like the sister they no longer remember having. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: bittersweet, the cost made flesh.

chapters.title: The Second Verse, Remembered
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ivy hums the lullaby's second verse—something she was never taught. In a thrift-store mirror, the woman who was Lena sees her reflection smile a half-second early, and hums along. POV: Ivy, closing on Lena. Emotional beat: ambiguous resolution—memory as haunting, love as residue.
